content: The relationship between breastfeeding duration and health outcomes was critically analyzed by the Guideline Development Group (GDG) of the World Health Organization (WHO). The manuscript underwent critical review and revision, including translation of non-English manuscripts. Contributions from authors were as follows: HPS, DS, and TG conceptualized and designed the study; TG and RKM conducted the literature search, data extraction, and entry; DS, TG, and RKM interpreted the data; HPS, TG, DS, and RKM performed data analysis; DS, TG, and RKM wrote the manuscript, with HPS providing critical inputs and interpretation. All authors approved the final manuscript. No conflicts of interest were declared by the authors. In studies examining shorter breastfeeding durations, most reported a range of 6–12 months. For studies reporting breastfeeding duration as a range, the minimum duration of 6–12 months was used as the comparison group. When data were available for breastfeeding durations of 9–12 months, 6–9 months, or 6–12 months, the 9–12-month group was preferred for comparison. Subgroup analyses were planned for child development and growth, stratified by breastfeeding duration in the second year (12–15 months, 15–18 months, 18–21 months, and 21–24 months). However, studies reporting only summary statistics for breastfeeding duration were excluded from these analyses. Additional subgroup analyses were planned based on the developmental status of the study population (high-income vs. lowand middle-income countries, as per World Bank classification), area of residence (rural vs. urban), and year of publication. Most studies with stratified data reported durations of 12–18 months and 18–24 months, leading to subgroup analyses being limited to these two groups. Subgroup analyses were performed for IQ scores, underweight, and overweight/obesity in children. However, subgroup analyses for other parameters could not be conducted due to insufficient studies in various subgroups for each outcome. Study Characteristics and Methodologies: 1. Abarca 2019: This cross-sectional study used data from the 2011–2012 National Survey of Children’s Health (NSCH) in the U.S., which included households with at least one child under 18 years of age. The study focused on children aged 3–5 years, with parents (primarily mothers) responding to questions about asthma, adverse childhood experiences, and breastfeeding duration and supplementation. Breastfeeding was categorized into four groups: exclusive breastfeeding up to 6 months, supplemental breastfeeding up to 6 months, supplemental breastfeeding for >6 to <12 months, and supplemental breastfeeding for ≥12 months. Children who were never breastfed served as the reference group. 2. Adair 1992: This cohort study followed women from 33 randomly selected barangays in Metro Cebu, Philippines, from the third trimester of pregnancy through 24 postpartum months. Inclusion criteria included delivering single live infants, with follow-up interviews and assessments conducted bimonthly. Excluded were participants who became pregnant again or missed more than two consecutive surveys. Breastfeeding patterns were categorized as weaned before 12 months, weaned between 12–24 months, or still breastfeeding at 24 months. Outcomes included postpartum weight changes. 3. Alho 1990: This cohort study in northern Finland enrolled children from 10 local government districts using block randomization. The study examined acute otitis media (AOM), respiratory tract infections (RTI), and wheezy bronchitis up to 2 years of age. Breastfeeding positions (supine, semi-supine, or upright) were also analyzed as potential risk factors for these conditions. 4. Al-Makoshi 2013: This cross-sectional study included 721 13-year-old children attending outpatient clinics in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as never, 0–3 months, 3–6 months, 6–12 months, and >12 months. 5. Araujo 2006: This cohort study in Pelotas, Brazil, followed hospital-delivered newborns from 1993, with follow-up visits at 6, 12, and 48 months. Breastfeeding patterns were classified by total duration, predominant breastfeeding, and ever breastfed. Outcomes included the prevalence of overweight and mean weight-for-height z-scores (WHZ) at 4 years. 6. Ardic 2018: This prospective cohort study in Rize, Turkey, included 411 children born between January and December 2011. Participants were divided into two groups based on breastfeeding duration (<12 months or ≥12 months). Outcomes included the incidence of infections up to 5 years of age. 7. Azevedo 2005: This cross-sectional study in Brazil included 369 preschool children aged 36–71 months from low-income areas. Data on infant feeding practices, including breastfeeding and bottle-feeding patterns, were collected through interviews and 24-hour recall diaries. Oral examinations were conducted to assess severe early childhood caries (SECC). 8. Bajaj 2017: This prospective cohort study in Canada evaluated the relationship between glucose tolerance during pregnancy and metabolic function postpartum. Breastfeeding duration was categorized as <3 months, 3–12 months, and >12 months. Outcomes included metabolic measures at 3 months, 1 year, and 3 years postpartum. 9. Belfort 2013: This prospective cohort study was part of Project Viva, which examined prenatal factors in relation to pregnancy and child health. Pregnant women were enrolled between 1999 and 2002 in Massachusetts. Exclusion criteria included multiple gestations, inability to answer questions in English, and missing breastfeeding or cognitive data. Outcomes included cognitive assessments at 3 and 7 years of age. Risk of Bias: Across studies, the risk of bias was frequently judged as unclear due to confounding, participant selection, classification of exposures, departures from intended exposures, incomplete outcome data, measurement of outcomes, selection of reported results, and other biases. Specific biases included unclear random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, and selective reporting.
